newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: Austrian far-right renews attack on EU.
newsitem.headline: Austrian far-right renews attack on EU.

text.p: Austrian Freedom Party leader Joerg Haider, poised for re-election as chief of Europe's biggest far-right grouping, roused the faithful on Saturday with a stinging attack on Brussels.
Haider told 600 delegates gathered for a party conference in this western town in the shadow of the Alps that a future single European currency would spell economic disaster for Austria.
He raised the spectre of social unrest if politicians pressed ahead with the scheme against the will of the people.
"Everyone is talking about Maastricht. The whole of Europe is being dictated by Maastricht and we are well on the way to carrying out a very dangerous experiment," he said in a key-note address.

"We want a Europe of people, not bureaucrats. We want a Europe that creates jobs, not chops them." His words were carried far beyond Feldkirch by an internet link to Freedom Party supporters across the country.

Earlier Haider had stopped in blazing sunshine to conduct a local brass band before making a triumphant entry into the packed hall, some 700 km (400 miles) west of Vienna and just a stone's throw from the Swiss border.

The Freedom Party scored its best election success to date in a European parliamentary poll on October 13, snapping at the heels of the ruling left-right coalition and picking up 27.6 percent of the vote from a public disillusioned by 21 months of EU membership.
"The political landscape has undergone a profound change and that was just the overture...Nothing will ever be the same again. Our time has come," Haider said to deafening applause.
Haider condemned the ruling Social Democrats and their junior coalition partner the conservative People's Party for attempting to exclude the Freedom Party from government.
"The brutal attempt to isolate the Freedom Party has failed. They cannot ignore more than one million voters," he said.
Haider rejected any cooperation with the People's Party, often cited in Austrian media as his most likely ally in a future government.
In his 10 years at the helm, the charismatic 46-year old leader has taken the Freedom Party from a marginal movement with little support to Europe's most influential far-right grouping.
On Saturday, Haider was at pains to claim the centre ground for the Freedom Party, which he said the foreign press had wrongly villified.
"The Freedom Party is comparable with Germany's CSU, France's Gaullists and the liberal parties of numerous countries," he said.
"We are nationalists. That means we want to defend our German language and our national identity in a big Europe. It does not mean we want to glorify nazism," he continued.

Haider pointed to the Freedom Party candidature of Jewish writer Peter Sichrovsky in the European election as proof of his party's liberal credentials. Sichrovsky's parents fled Austria and the Nazis during the Second World War.

"In our ranks are academics, professionals and the self-employed. The future belongs to us," said Haider, who in 1991 was forced to resign as provincial governor of Carinthia after parising Adolf Hitler's labour policies.
